archetypes.name: Pyramidal horn (optimum gain)
archetypes.summary: Rectangular waveguide flared in both planes, proportioned for maximum gain at a given length.

synthesis.notes: Equal-slant approximation rho_e = rho_h = rho. Substituting the optimum-gain conditions into G = 0.51*4*pi*a1*b1/lambda^2 gives G0 = 15.6984*rho/lambda exactly.

analysis.notes: Forward check against the synthesised aperture; must return G_target. 0.51 is the standard optimum-pyramidal aperture efficiency, which already embeds the quadratic phase-error loss over the flared aperture.
E-plane HPBW = 54.1*lambda/b1 for an optimum horn
H-plane HPBW = 78.1*lambda/a1 for an optimum horn
Independent cross-check via D ~ 26000/(theta_E*theta_H). Agrees with the aperture formula to about 0.18 dB, which is the honest accuracy of both.
s = b1^2/(8*lambda*rho_e); the optimum design fixes this at 0.25
t = a1^2/(8*lambda*rho_h); the optimum design fixes this at 0.375

validity: optimum-gain proportions only; a horn of arbitrary a1/b1/rho needs the full Fresnel-integral gain expression (Balanis 13-19), not this closed form

the equal-slant simplification rho_e = rho_h is exact for the standard design but a physically realisable pyramidal horn also requires the two flare sections to meet at the waveguide, which constrains rho_e and rho_h separately
G_target above about 30 dBi gives a horn long enough that a reflector is usually the better answer
does not model the waveguide-to-horn junction mismatch

known_cases.source: Self-consistency across independent routes: the optimum-gain dimensions must reproduce the requested gain through G = 0.51*4*pi*a1*b1/lambda^2, and must land on the canonical phase errors s = 1/4 and t = 3/8. Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 13
20 dBi at 10 GHz: a1 = 4.3715 lambda, b1 = 3.5693 lambda; HPBW 15.16 deg (E) and 17.87 deg (H). Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 13
Cross-check: D ~ 26000/(theta_E*theta_H) must agree with the aperture-area gain to within the ~0.2 dB accuracy of the beamwidth approximation. Milligan, Modern Antenna Design 2nd ed., Ch. 7

references: Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 13 (13.4.3, optimum pyramidal horn design)
Milligan, Modern Antenna Design 2nd ed., Ch. 7

archetypes.name: E-plane sectoral horn (optimum)
archetypes.summary: Rectangular waveguide flared in the E-plane only; the H-plane keeps the waveguide's cosine distribution.

analysis.notes: aperture efficiency 0.65 for the optimum E-plane horn

validity: optimum flare only
the exact gain needs Fresnel integrals (Balanis 13-19/13-41); this closed form is the standard optimum-design shortcut
aperture efficiency figure is the textbook value for the optimum case and does not track departures from it

known_cases.source: b1 = sqrt(2*lambda*rho) at 10 GHz with rho = 0.3 m. Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 13

archetypes.name: H-plane sectoral horn (optimum)
archetypes.summary: Rectangular waveguide flared in the H-plane only; the E-plane keeps the waveguide's uniform distribution.

analysis.notes: aperture efficiency 0.64 for the optimum H-plane horn

validity: optimum flare only
the exact gain needs Fresnel integrals (Balanis 13-19/13-41); this closed form is the standard optimum-design shortcut
aperture efficiency figure is the textbook value for the optimum case and does not track departures from it

known_cases.source: a1 = sqrt(3*lambda*rho) at 10 GHz with rho = 0.3 m. Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 13

archetypes.name: Conical horn (optimum gain)
archetypes.summary: Circular waveguide flared into a cone; the standard reflector feed.

analysis.notes: aperture efficiency 0.51, as for the pyramidal horn
approximately 60*lambda/d_m; the conical horn's E- and H-plane beamwidths differ by roughly 10%, which is why cross-polarisation is poor

validity: optimum flare only
TE11 dominant mode
asymmetric pattern and high cross-polarisation; use a corrugated horn where pattern symmetry matters

known_cases.source: d_m = sqrt(3*lambda*L) = 164.2 mm at 10 GHz, L = 0.3 m; G = 0.51*4*pi*A/lambda^2. Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 13

archetypes.name: Corrugated (scalar) conical horn
archetypes.summary: Conical horn with lambda/4 corrugations, giving a symmetric HE11 balanced-hybrid pattern.

synthesis.notes: lambda/4 slots present a high surface impedance, which is what enforces the balanced-hybrid HE11 condition. Depth must hold across the band, so wideband designs taper it from lambda/2 at the throat to lambda/4 at the aperture.

analysis.notes: aperture efficiency 0.69, materially better than the 0.51 of a smooth-wall horn
the same in both planes, which is the whole point of the corrugations
Indicative: well-made corrugated horns reach -30 dB or better across the design band

validity: at least 5 corrugations per wavelength; below that the surface-impedance model fails
balanced-hybrid condition holds over roughly an octave; wider needs a tapered slot depth
cross-polarisation figure is indicative, not derived

known_cases.source: Same aperture as the smooth conical horn, lambda/4 = 7.49 mm slots, and 10*log10(0.69/0.51) = 1.32 dB of aperture-efficiency advantage. Clarricoats & Olver, Corrugated Horns for Microwave Antennas

references: Clarricoats & Olver, Corrugated Horns for Microwave Antennas

archetypes.name: Open-ended rectangular waveguide
archetypes.summary: Unflared waveguide aperture; the low-gain limit of the horn family.

analysis.notes: exactly 8/pi^2 = 0.8106 for the TE10 cosine distribution across a, uniform across b
ignores the aperture mismatch, which is significant for an unflared guide
TE10 guide wavelength; diverges at cutoff

validity: single-mode TE10 operation: f0 between the TE10 and TE20 cutoffs
aperture reflection is neglected, so the gain figure is optimistic by a few tenths of a dB
an infinite ground plane is assumed; a bare guide end radiates backward as well

known_cases.source: WR-90 (22.86 x 10.16 mm) at 10 GHz: TE10 cutoff = c/(2a) = 6.556 GHz; aperture is only 0.76 x 0.34 lambda, so G = (8/pi^2)*4*pi*A/lambda^2 = 4.20 dBi. Published ~6 dBi figures for open-ended guide usually include a flange. Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 13

archetypes.name: Diagonal horn
archetypes.summary: Square aperture carrying two orthogonal modes in phase, radiating a symmetric beam polarised along the diagonal.

analysis.notes: DERIVED, not tabulated: for E = y*cos(pi*x/a) + x*cos(pi*y/a), the co-polar aperture efficiency along the diagonal works out to exactly 8/pi^2 = 0.8106. A separable cos*cos aperture would give only 64/pi^4 = 0.657, so the diagonal horn is genuinely more efficient than a pyramidal one.
uniform phase across the aperture, i.e. an infinitely long horn
Quadratic phase error at the aperture corner, (a/2)^2/(2R) expressed in wavelengths. Keep it under about 1/8 for the ideal gain to be realised.
R >= a^2/lambda holds the corner phase error to an eighth of a wavelength
Indicative and equal in both principal planes, which is the horn's selling point - a pyramidal horn's E and H beamwidths differ by a third

Exactly zero on boresight: the cross-polar aperture integral cancels by symmetry, confirmed numerically to 1e-17. Off boresight four cross-polar lobes appear in the diagonal planes, typically around -19 dB, and those are NOT modelled here.
0.91 dB, from 8/pi^2 against the separable aperture's 64/pi^4

validity: the two modes must be equal in amplitude and phase at the aperture, which happens at one frequency band only - the diagonal horn is not broadband
gain assumes uniform phase; check max_phase_error_wavelengths and lengthen the horn if it exceeds about 0.125
polarisation is along the DIAGONAL of the square aperture, not along a side
the diagonal-plane cross-polar lobes are real and significant; only the boresight null is claimed here

known_cases.source: 8/pi^2 = 0.810569, derived by integrating the two-mode aperture field and confirmed on a 2001x2001 grid (0.810974). A 60 mm aperture at 10 GHz is 2 wavelengths square, so 4*pi*A/lambda^2 = 50.34 and the gain is 0.8106*50.34 = 40.80 = 16.11 dBi.
(a/2)^2/(2R) = 0.9 mm = 0.075 wavelengths at 10 GHz, comfortably inside the eighth-wave rule, which would allow a horn as short as 120 mm
10*log10((8/pi^2)/(64/pi^4)) = 10*log10(pi^2/8) = 0.914 dB over a separable cosine aperture

references: Love, The diagonal horn antenna, Microwave Journal 5, 1962
Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 13 for the aperture-integration method
Aperture efficiency derived and numerically confirmed here

archetypes.name: Dual-mode (Potter) conical horn
archetypes.summary: A step in a conical horn launches TM11 alongside TE11, cancelling the aperture's cross-polar field over a narrow band.

parameters.name: TM11 amplitude fraction
parameters.description: relative to TE11; the classic Potter design sits near 0.15

synthesis.notes: optimum-gain conical relation, the same one the smooth and corrugated horns in this family use

INDICATIVE. The step must sit where TE11 propagates and TM11 is just above cutoff - TM11 cuts off at d = 1.22*lambda in a circular guide, so a diameter a little above that is where the mode is launched. The exact diameter and step height set the TM11 fraction and need a mode-matching solve.

analysis.notes: INDICATIVE AND NOT DERIVED. Placed between this family's smooth conical horn (0.51) and corrugated horn (0.69), which is where published Potter horns land. The dual-mode horn's purpose is pattern symmetry and cross-polar purity, not gain.
0.85 dB, and that is the smaller part of the benefit
Indicative, and equal in E and H planes - the symmetry the mode mixture buys. A smooth conical horn differs by about 10 degrees between planes.

INDICATIVE, at the design frequency only. Good Potter horns reach -30 dB or better at band centre and degrade to -20 dB within a few percent either side, because TE11 and TM11 travel at different phase velocities and drift out of step.
TM11 cuts off where k*a equals the first zero of J1, 3.8317, i.e. d = 1.2197*lambda. Below this diameter the second mode cannot exist and the horn is simply a smooth one.
TE11 cuts off at the first zero of J1', 1.8412, giving d = 0.5861*lambda

INDICATIVE. The cross-polar cancellation is a phase condition between two modes with different dispersion, so it holds over a few percent. Corrugated horns achieve the same symmetry over an octave, which is why they displaced this design for wideband feeds.

validity: LOW CONFIDENCE: aperture efficiency, cross-polar level, beamwidth constant and bandwidth are all indicative figures placed by analogy with the neighbouring horn archetypes, not computed
the step geometry is not solved - setting the TM11 fraction to a target needs mode matching, which this spec does not attempt
narrowband by construction: the mode phase relationship holds at one frequency
the two cutoff diameters ARE exact, being Bessel zeros; treat them as the reliable part of this spec

known_cases.source: Exact circular-waveguide cutoffs from the Bessel zeros: TM11 at j(1,1) = 3.8317 gives d = 1.2197*lambda, TE11 at j'(1,1) = 1.8412 gives d = 0.5861*lambda. At 10 GHz, 36.57 mm and 17.57 mm. Cross-checked against this toolkit's circular waveguide module.

sqrt(3*lambda*L) = 164.26 mm for a 300 mm horn at 10 GHz, identical to the smooth conical horn of the same length. The gain advantage is 10*log10(0.62/0.51) = 0.85 dB - modest, and not the reason to build one.

references: Potter, A new horn antenna with suppressed sidelobes and equal beamwidths, Microwave Journal 6, 1963
Milligan, Modern Antenna Design 2nd ed., Ch. 7
Balanis, Antenna Theory 4th ed., Ch. 13.4 for the conical horn basis
